doc.title: Ray Bryant interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Touring Japan and the Blues Brothers with Junior Mance
summary: Solo tours and the One Hundred Gold Fingers show in Japan, where he and Junior Mance became the Blues Brothers.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Jazz certainly has its own language, and it’s marvelous to see veterans working together, that they’ve all done it so many times. They can be in a New York venue like that and pull it off. It’s great. I know you’ve traveled overseas quite a bit.
The Japanese in particular seem to really enjoy jazz. You go over there once a year or—

Well at least once a year generally. Sometimes there have been years where I’ve gone three times within one year. But generally maybe once or twice a year I do solo tours over there, and the last maybe five or six years there’s been a production, a Japanese production over there, called One Hundred Gold Fingers, and they bring over ten of us. Ten piano players on the same show. And it’s very successful in Japan. I don’t know really how well it would do over here in the United States. But the Japanese promoter has been thinking about it, because it’s really been successful over there. And then I go do a festival once in a while or something like that. Or I go over just to record once in a while. But I’ve been to Japan many, many times and it’s a good place to go and play jazz. People really love it. I look forward to going back again.
A friend of yours, Junior Mance, told me to ask you about the Blues Brothers.

Well within this production, the One Hundred Gold Fingers, you get to play duets, you know you play your solo piano, you play duets with other people. Marian did it once with us, she went over one year. The roster varies, they change it around from year to year. But I’ve been on every one every year, I’ve been on every one, Junior has too. So I guess it was inevitable, in the pairing up of different piano players like playing duets, Junior and I would end up together at least. So we did it once and we played the blues and the reception was so great that pretty soon Junior and I sort of found ourselves together most of the time, and we played the blues. And so that’s why the Blues Brothers. They started calling us the Blues Brothers.
